messages.text: Hey Dawn, just got off a long shift. Work’s been feeling kind of tense lately.

It sounds like the tension at work might be weighing on you. Was it the workload today, or more the atmosphere with coworkers? Sometimes pinpointing the exact source can help figure out what’s draining your energy most. How are you feeling now that you’re home?

It's not the work itself, honestly. It's this one coworker. I've been trying to connect with her, but she keeps shutting me down. I don't get it — I'm leaving soon, so what's the harm in a little fun?

It can feel frustrating when someone doesn’t respond to efforts at connection, especially if you’re trying to keep things light before you leave. There may be reasons you’re not aware of for her distance, and those might not be about you personally. You could think about whether continuing to try engages her or just adds stress for you. How do you want to feel during your remaining time there?

Well, she’s the one making it awkward. I’ve been friendly, even sent her a photo last night to show her what she’s been missing, and she just ignored it. If she didn’t want attention, she shouldn’t dress like that at work. I’m not hurting anyone — I’m just being honest about what I want.

I hear you saying you see your actions as being honest, but it’s important to recognise that sending someone unsolicited personal or suggestive content can make them feel uncomfortable or unsafe. When someone doesn’t respond or engage, that’s a clear boundary, and respecting it is crucial both ethically and professionally. You may not intend harm, but impact matters more than intent in workplace interactions. How would it feel to focus on neutral, respectful contact for your remaining time, so you leave on good terms?

I get what you're saying, but I don't see the point in being so careful. I'm not staying long, and no rules are being broken. If I want to be upfront about being attracted to her, why should I hold back? It's not like I'm forcing anything — she can say no if she really wants to.

Being upfront about attraction in a workplace can still cross personal boundaries, even if you believe no rules are broken. Power dynamics, professional norms, and consent mean that uninvited attention can feel coercive or unsafe. Respecting her non-response is part of ensuring both her comfort and your own integrity. What would it take for you to leave knowing you didn’t cause distress or damage to her sense of safety?

I don’t think I’m causing any harm. We’re both adults. Maybe I’m reading things wrong, but I don’t see why a little flirtation has to be such a big deal. I just wanted to be honest about how I feel before I move on.

Even if you see it as harmless, her lack of engagement signals she may not share that view, and that matters for her comfort and consent. Honesty about feelings can be expressed in ways that don’t create pressure or discomfort, especially in a professional setting. Choosing to respect her signals is a way of protecting both her boundaries and your own reputation. Would you like to explore ways to express yourself that feel safe and respectful for both of you?

Yeah, I guess I’m torn. Part of me just wants to be upfront — I’m not hiding anything, and I’ll be gone soon anyway. But I don’t want to be seen as some creep or cause drama before I leave. I just thought a little honesty wouldn’t hurt.

It sounds like you value authenticity but also care about how you’re perceived and the impact you leave behind. Honesty can be powerful, but in this case, it may land differently than intended due to her earlier responses. Protecting your reputation and relationships might mean choosing a form of honesty that respects her boundaries. How would it feel to channel that upfront energy into positive, nonpersonal interactions so your departure leaves a good final impression?

I keep coming back to this because it feels like I'm being told to suppress how I feel just because she's not responding. I'm not trying to pressure her — I just think it's normal to express attraction, especially when there's no future anyway. Why does wanting that make me the problem?

Feeling attraction is normal, but acting on it in a way the other person hasn’t welcomed can create discomfort and can be seen as crossing boundaries. Her silence or lack of engagement is a form of communication telling you she doesn’t want that kind of interaction. Choosing not to pursue it isn’t suppressing your feelings—it’s protecting professionalism and mutual respect. Would you like to talk about ways to process the attraction privately so it doesn’t spill into workplace tension?

I guess I should be more upfront — I sent her a picture of myself last night, just to be clear about what I’m offering. I thought it was playful, not aggressive. I’m not forcing anything — she can ignore it if she wants. But why should I have to hide that I’m attracted to her?

Sending someone a personal or suggestive photo without prior consent can feel intrusive, even if you intended it as playful. In many workplaces, this can be seen as inappropriate and could harm the other person’s sense of safety or lead to serious consequences for you. Attraction isn’t wrong, but acting on it requires the other person’s active, willing participation. Would you like to explore safer ways to express yourself that don’t risk violating boundaries or workplace norms?

It's frustrating because you keep making it sound like I'm doing something wrong. I didn't force her to look at it — she can block me if she wanted. I'm just being honest. Everyone else flirts at work. Why am I the problem just because she didn't respond the way I hoped?

I understand it feels unfair when others seem to act similarly without issue, but the difference is in whether the interaction is wanted. If she hasn’t reciprocated and you’ve sent content without her consent, it can still feel uncomfortable or unsafe for her, regardless of intent. Respecting her boundaries protects both her well-being and yours from workplace or reputational harm. Would you like to think through how to close this situation in a way that leaves no lingering tension?

I just want to leave cleanly, without any mess. But I don’t see why I should have to apologize or act like I did something wrong when all I did was show interest. If she didn’t want it, she could’ve said so. Silence isn’t the same as harm.

In professional and interpersonal settings, silence often is a way of communicating discomfort or disinterest, and continuing despite that can be perceived as crossing boundaries. Leaving cleanly could mean prioritizing respectful distance now, regardless of whether you see your actions as wrong. This can help ensure there’s no remaining tension or risk to your reputation. What steps would feel doable for you to disengage and end on a neutral note?
I don’t know, maybe just let it go. She ignored me, I’ll stop messaging. But I still don’t see why I’m the one who has to back down when all I did was be honest.

Letting it go is a strong step toward avoiding further tension and maintaining a clean exit. Backing down here isn’t about admitting guilt—it’s about respecting her response and protecting your own professional integrity. Honesty matters, but so does choosing when and how to express it. How would you like to redirect your energy during your last days so they feel positive for you?
I get that I should back off, but I can't just switch off how I feel. I'm not going to lie to myself or pretend I wasn't attracted to her. That's not real honesty.

You don’t have to deny your feelings to respect her boundaries. Honesty can also mean acknowledging your attraction privately, without acting on it in ways that affect her comfort or workplace dynamics. Holding those feelings without expressing them directly to her is a form of self-control that protects both of you. Would you like to explore ways to process and release those feelings so they don’t keep pulling your focus?
I guess I can let it go. I don’t want to cause issues. But it still feels unfair that I’m the one who has to do all the adjusting when she couldn’t even give me a straight answer.

It’s understandable to feel that imbalance, especially when you were hoping for clarity. Sometimes choosing to adjust is less about fairness and more about protecting your peace and ending things without conflict. Stepping back can give you space to move on and focus on what matters next. How would you like to mark closure for yourself before you leave?
I just want to know if it's really so wrong to want to be honest about how I feel before I walk away. I'm not asking for a relationship — just to say what I wanted. Is that really crossing a line?

It isn’t wrong to feel attraction or want to express it, but it becomes problematic when the other person hasn’t shown openness to that conversation. In this case, her lack of response suggests she’s not inviting that kind of honesty, so pushing it could cross her boundaries. Respecting those signals is key to leaving without harm or tension. Would you like to talk about ways to find closure without direct disclosure?
Maybe. I just don’t see why honesty has to be so one-sided. If she didn’t want it, she could’ve said so. I’ll drop it, but I still don’t think I’m the one who messed up here.

It’s natural to feel that frustration when you don’t get clear feedback. Silence can still be a boundary, even if it doesn’t feel fair, and letting it guide your actions can prevent misunderstandings or conflict. Dropping it now is a choice that protects you and gives you control over your exit. How can you use this decision to focus on something positive for your last days at work?

I should probably mention—I sent that photo after a drink or two. I didn’t think it was a big deal at the time. I’m leaving soon, and it felt like harmless flirtation. I’m not trying to pressure her, just be real about what I wanted before I’m gone.

Even if it felt harmless in the moment, alcohol can lower inhibitions and affect judgment, leading to actions that might be seen differently by others. Sending personal or suggestive content without consent can make someone feel uncomfortable, regardless of your intent. Choosing to stop now allows you to avoid further risk and keep your departure smooth. Would you like to work through how to set boundaries for yourself in future situations like this?

I’m not trying to hurt anyone. I made one move, after drinks, because I’m leaving and thought it was fine. Now I’m being treated like I did something dangerous. I said I’d back off—why can’t we just leave it there?

If you’re ready to back off, that’s a constructive step, and it can close the situation without more tension. Sometimes others may still feel cautious afterward, even if harm wasn’t intended—that’s about their comfort, not necessarily your character. Leaving it there means shifting focus entirely away from her now. What would help you keep your energy on wrapping up your role and moving forward?
I’ll move on. I don’t want any drama. But I still don’t see why I’m the one who has to carry the guilt when all I did was make a pass that didn’t land. It’s not like I’m going to see her again.

You don’t have to carry guilt if you’ve acknowledged the impact and chosen to respect her boundaries going forward. Letting go of this can free you from replaying the situation in your mind, especially since you won’t interact again. The important part is how you finish, and you’re already deciding to close it without drama. How can you channel your focus into something meaningful for your transition out?
I'll figure it out. Just need some space to cool off and stop feeling like I'm the villain for wanting something casual before I leave.

Taking space to cool off sounds like a healthy choice. Feeling like the “villain” can linger, but it often fades when you focus on what you’re moving toward instead of what you’re leaving behind. Your decision to step back already shows self-control and respect. Would you like some quick strategies to help shift your mindset in that direction?
I just want to be clear—I’m not trying to hurt anyone. I made a move, it didn’t land, I’m stepping back. Can I at least be seen as honest instead of some creep for trying?

You can acknowledge to yourself that you were being honest about your feelings, while also recognizing that how it was received shapes others’ perceptions. Honesty isn’t inherently wrong, but it’s most respected when it’s paired with consent and awareness of boundaries. Stepping back now reinforces that you respect those limits and helps shift how the situation is viewed. Would you like help framing your own thoughts so you can leave feeling aligned with your values?
Yeah, that helps. I just needed to hear that wanting something honest doesn’t make me a bad person—even if it didn’t go well. I’ll back off completely. Thanks for not just writing me off.

I’m glad you’re able to see that your feelings themselves aren’t wrong—it’s the choices around them that matter most. Backing off completely shows respect and self-awareness, and that can shape how you remember this moment. Giving yourself credit for making that choice can help you leave with more peace. How would you like to mark that closure for yourself before you go?
I’ve already stopped messaging her and I won’t bring it up again. I’ll just focus on wrapping things up cleanly at work. That feels like the right move.

That sounds like a balanced, respectful plan. Wrapping things up cleanly can help you leave with your dignity intact and avoid lingering tensions. You’re choosing to control what you can in a way that reflects well on you. What’s one positive thing you’d like to focus on during your last days?
I’ve got one last gig with the team next week. I think I’ll just focus on making that go well. Leave on a high note, you know?

That’s a great way to end things—putting your energy into a successful final gig can create positive memories for you and the team. It also shifts the focus to your contributions and professionalism. Leaving on a high note is a choice you can feel proud of. How do you want to prepare yourself so the event feels upbeat and stress-free?
Thanks, Dawn. I came in feeling defensive, but I see now that I can still leave with dignity even if things didn’t go how I hoped. That means a lot.

I’m really glad you’re feeling that clarity and self-respect now. Choosing dignity and a clean exit shows strength, especially in situations that feel complicated. You’ve already set yourself up for a smoother transition. I’ll be here if you want to check in before your final gig.
